Press Release:


Superbugs
When you go into a hospital healthy and end up severely ill with an antibiotic resistant superbug, who should be held responsible? These so-called superbugs are spreading across South African hospitals at an alarming rate, increasing infections. Carte Blanche investigates how these bacteria are managing to thrive in private hospital theatres and what forms of prevention are out there for patients.
Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender
Researcher: Laura Byrnes

Script:


When you go into a hospital for surgery, you’re asked to sign a consent form full of disclaimers, but do you understand what you may be in for?
SOURCE: “At least 30% of all superbugs are stemming from the theatre environment. It’s a very dirty secret.”
Roy: “I wouldn’t wish this on my worst enemy.”
“Superbugs,” it’s a menacing word. And when we asked viewers about them we received stories around the country claiming to have drug resistant infections, some of which appear on the World Health Organization’s superbug hot list. Academic head of clinical care at Wits, Professor Guy Richards is an Intensivist at Charlotte Maxeke.
Dr. Richards: “We're the people that look after the sickest patients in intensive care units.”
The bacteria behind these infections mutates, becoming resistant to the dozens of antibiotics developed to wage war against them.
Dr. Richards: “We talk about organisms which are only MDR, that multi drug resistant, XDR, where they are sensitive to only one or two anti-biotic, and PDR, which is pan drug resistant, which means they’re resistant to all anti-biotics.”
Hospital patients who are already sick are at a greater risk for an infection because their immune systems are suppressed.
Dr. Richards: “You have packed together large numbers of patients that are receiving a large amount of antibiotics, therefore, those in the hospital are always potentially much more resistant than those that are in the community.”
Devi: “Is there an increase in the number of these bugs that exist in hospitals?”
Dr. Richards: “Absolutely, all over the world.”
LINK: “BUGS ARE GETTING SMARTER, THEY TALK TO EACH OTHER, ITS CALLED CHORUM SENSING, WHERE THEY SHARE INFORMATION WITH EACH OTHER ABOUT HOW TO ATTACK OR INVADE A PART OF THE BODY.”
According to the national institute for communicable diseases, last year in the public sector, in just over a quarter of a million (254 592) blood samples, 9% tested positive for superbug cultures. The problem lies with the over-prescription of antibiotics.
Dr. Richards: “They’re still used worse in private than they are in state, because we restrict access to many of the broader spectrum agents in state.”
LINK: IT’S ONE THING WHEN YOU’RE ADMITTED INTO A HOSPITAL WITH A PRE-EXISTING CONDITION, IT’S SOMETHING ELSE WHEN YOU COME IN HEALTHY, AND YOU LEAVE WORSE THAN YOU WERE BEFORE.
Although an infection’s origin cannot be determined, it’s well documented that they lurk in hospitals around the world including South Africa. At Life’s Westville hospital in Durban, Roy Lorentz, who lost his arm in a previous accident, underwent knee replacement surgery.
Roy: “It was 2-3 days after the operation, it started weeping and there was a gaping big hole.”
What started as a surgical site infection, was later diagnosed as pseudomonas, a superbug typically found in hospitals. His daughter, Liesel Manggos, says he’s had 14 surgeries and spent over 200 days in hospital.
Liesel: “Never for one minute do you expect a health man to go in for a knee operation, and then to come out with a hospital acquired infection, that 4 years later has not been cured.”
Life Hospital Group said in writing they regret Roy’s years of suffering and his case was taken very seriously. Their thorough investigation revealed there was no breach by them of strong infection protection measures.
At Morningside Mediclinic in Johannesburg, June Walsh’s hip surgery left her in pain, and 21 months later she was diagnosed with Staphloccocus Epidermis, and Streptococcus viridans.
June: “It was down in the femur where the prosthesis was. I landed up being over the bucket for 4 weeks.”
In total, June spent nearly a month in isolation.
Source: “The healthcare industry is failing the patients that they’re supposed to be caring for.”
“SARAH” is a medical professional with clinical experience and more than 20 years in the industry. She is speaking to us anonymously for fear of backlash.
Devi: “Should the hospitals not be held liable for that duration, for that particular part of the stay?”
Source: “Unfortunately there’s no evidence or proof that you didn’t come into the hospital with that superbug.”
Devi: “In fairness to hospitals too.” (Hmhm)
Medical negligence experts say infections are documented as “complications” by the hospitals; and signing a consent form, makes it difficult to hold the hospital responsible. This lack of power to hold anyone responsible is why June became depressed while in isolation.
Devi: “At some point you became suicidal?”
June: “I had ten drips on me. I had to have a little bowl where they were draining out the poison out of the, my here, and it burnt down my leg.”
Mediclinic say in writing their investigation shows June’s infections are not hospital associated as they weren’t identified within 30-90 days of her surgery and aren’t related to it. But, medical experts we consulted say that prosthesis infections are hard to diagnose and usually these infections are hospital acquired.
Mediclinic also say June’s infections were not multidrug resistant, but her blood results show they were resistant to some antibiotics.
Sarah says any theater environment is where the risk of contamination is at it’s highest, especially when unqualified medical device representatives are illegally aiding surgeons during operations – like this rep who hands over a medical device to a surgeon without wearing gloves.
Source: “They might be assisting the surgeon by holding the leg, manipulating the leg. There’s even been cases of salespeople drilling and sawing in patients.”
Devi: “Internationally, will medical reps be present in procedures there too?”
Source: “It’s absolutely against the law for a medical rep to assist. It’s against the law in SA too.”
There are meant to be strict protocols to keep the theater environment sterile, but these are not always adhered to. This undercover footage was taken inside two private hospital theatres in Gauteng. Doors are seen left open, exposing the patients to unpurified air. Reps can be seen moving theater equipment and leaning over patients. Or wearing shoes without covers, which is not proper theatre attire. This rep opens up a device’s packaging without gloves. According to Sarah, these common oversights happen in all hospitals, and increase the risk of contracting a superbug.
Source: “I’m not saying hospitals don’t care about superbugs, they will do their utmost to isolate and clean the rooms.”
Cleaning an infected room thoroughly is a top priority at both private and public hospitals.
Dr Richards: “When we do have a highly resistant organism, we will then disinfect the ward with a fogger with hydrogen peroxide, to kill environmental organisms as well.”
Treating these infections is a costly exercise for the patient, Roy’s family estimates his superbug related hospital bill was roughly 4.2 million rand.
Roy: “I would say that the cost of plasters alone, was 10-15 thousand rand.”
June’s daughter Jessica Smith says to cover her hospital bills, her mother had to sell her home and car.
Jessica: “Now, she’s having to live with us and it’s hard. Financially, it’s well over a million.”
Source: “In my opinion it’s being pushed under the rug, because superbugs generate an income.”
Internationally studies show that surgical site infections can almost double the patients length of stay and cost of treatment. Infections are a minimum prescribed benefit in South Africa, and your medical aid must covers these costs. Discovery’s Head of Strategic Risk Management Dr. Roshini Moodley says last year the estimated direct cost to Discovery of Superbugs was R3 billion.
Discovery: “About 100 million rand of the 3 billion is spent on the antibiotics, year after year we’re seeing a 5-10% increase, there,fore the conclusion would be that there are more superbugs.”
Netcare’s Medical Director Anchen Laubser says their multitude of prevention measures – including the use of sterilizing robots - are capital intensive.
Anchen: “There’s absolutely no incentive in getting a patient to develop a complication, in fact it’s completely contra-to our values in Netcare.
Life Hospital group says the negative reputational and financial implications are powerful reasons to prevent infections.
Mediclinic say they have infection prevention and control managers and an electronic surveillance system that identifies infected patients.
LINK: YOU’RE FEELING A BIT FLUISH, SO YOU GO THE GP, BUT WITH THE EXPECTATION THAT YOU WILL LEAVE WITH A SCRIPT FOR AN ANTI-BIOTIC. THAT EXPECTATION IS ONE OF THE REASONS WHY BUGS ARE BECOMING MORE AND MORE DRUG RESISTANT.
Devi: Does it weaken your system?
Richards: “The taking of anti-biotic regularly, doesn’t change your immunity.”
It allows the pathogens to mutate to the antibiotics, increasing the risk of further resistance to develop. Because of this, it’s humanity’s responsibility to protect the anti-biotics we have left.
Dr. Richards: “Limit the use of the antibiotics, decrease the duration, use appropriate doses.”
LINK: SO HOW DO YOU PROTECT YOURSELF? IT’S SIMPLE. START BY DISINFECTING YOUR HANDS.
Roshini: “Vaccines also a very important area of preventing. If you prevent the infection, you prevent the antibiotic, you then you prevent a superbug developing.”
Devi: “Who needs to take responsibility for this?”
Source: “The whole healthcare industry needs to take responsibility for this.”
It’s too late for Roy, he still needs his wound redressed once a week.
Roy: “So they removed the knee totally. My leg is 10 cm shorter than it was. I suppose I have to live with it.” 10:18
